newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-Belgacom IPO report gets the cold shoulder.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Belgacom IPO report gets the cold shoulder.

text.p: A reported proposal by Belgian telephone company Belgacom for a $2 billion plus initial public offer for the state's 50.1 percent stake was swiftly torpedoed by authorities on Tuesday.
"For the time being, no initial public offering has been planned since this decision is up to the shareholders," chief executive officer John Goossens said in a statement.
Belgian Telecommunications Minister Elio Di Rupo flatly ruled out any further privatisation of Belgacom, at least for as long as he would be around.
The Wall Street Journal Europe said on Tuesday senior Belgacom managers urged the government to sell its controlling stake partly to help cover huge unfunded pension liabilities.
"As long as Di Rupo is Telecommunications minister, Belgacom will stay majority public (held)," Di Rupo's spokesman Marc Janssen told Reuters.
"Some may have a different opinion but (Di Rupo) is the minister who is responsible for the company and he has always said he'll oppose any widening of the privatisation," he said.
Both the Wall Street Journal and Belgian daily Financieel Economische Tijd said that according to the plan, the substantial capital gain yielded by the IPO would be injected to the Pension Fund.
Goossens told Tijd that Belgacom management was forced to look for a solution for the company's competitive handicaps.
The newspaper added Belgacom was the only telephone operator which had to carry its pension liabilities itself.
Belgacom paid 17 billion francs ($490 million) to the pension fund in 1996 for its 9,500 retired employees.

But the company will soon have to pay for an additional 5,000 to 6,000 people who are expected to accept an early retirement offer as part of a major restructuring programme which aims to cut the total workforce to 20,000.
The Pension Fund had 63 billion francs at the end of December 1996, but the Tijd said the Fund needed 160 billion francs according to international standards.
Goossens said in the statement it was management's concern however to remain competitive.
"In this respect, it is important...that company costs be decreased. A partial decrease in its contribution to the Pension Fund would help in this effort," he said.
He told Tijd that politicians' attitude towards Belgacom had changed and that the state was now just involved in major decisions, which require a 75-percent majority of the votes.
"That's why it does not make much difference whether (the state) owns 50.1 percent or 25 percent in Belgacom," he said.
He said foreign examples showed that the state could even yield 99.9 percent without losing its grip on the most strategic decisions "on the one condition it acquires a 'golden' share".
The rest of Belgacom's capital -- 49.9 percent -- is currently owned by a consortium including Ameritech, Singapore Telecom, TeleDanmark and three Belgian investors.

Ameritech has repeatedly said it aimed to raise its stake in Belgacom and the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) advised the Belgian state last month to sell off its remaining interests in Belgacom.
($ = 35.02 Belgian Francs)
